\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Telugu, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

A first real exchange — give your name, ask for someone else's, say you are glad to meet them. Built the same way as the greetings: each piece taken apart, its letters and its root, then assembled. \te{నా} \te{పేరు} \te{అరుణ్}. / \te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pēru]{\te{పేరు} (pēru) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} the native Dravidian word}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-peru}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian, even in Sanskrit-loving Telugu.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)} \textbf{\te{ప}} (pa) + \textbf{\te{ే}} (the \emph{ē}-sign) $\to$ \textbf{\te{పే}} (pē); \textbf{\te{రు}} (ru). Read \textbf{\te{పే}·\te{రు}} $\to$ \textbf{pēru}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{పేరు}} (\emph{pēru}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{native Dravidian}, from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pēr} — the same word as Tamil \emph{peyar} and Malayalam \emph{pēr}, and a cousin of Kannada \emph{hesaru} (which softened \emph{p} $\to$ \emph{h}). It is \emph{not} Sanskrit \emph{nāma} (Hindi \emph{nām}, English \emph{name}). Even Telugu — the most Sanskritised of the Dravidian tongues — kept its home-grown word for \textquotedblleft{}name.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Across the family — the same idea, six ways:}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{\te{పేరు}} \emph{pēru} & \textbf{native Dravidian} (*pēr) \\
Tamil & \emph{peyar} & the \emph{same} Dravidian root \\
Malayalam & \emph{pēr} & the \emph{same} Dravidian root \\
Kannada & \emph{hesaru} & Dravidian (*pesar, \emph{p} $\to$ \emph{h}) \\
Hindi & \emph{nām} & Sanskrit (Indo-European) \\
English & \emph{name} & Indo-European \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four Dravidian tongues, one inherited word — even Kannada's \emph{hesaru}, once you know the old \emph{p} went soft. Only the last two rows come from somewhere else.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{ప} (\emph{pa}) + \te{ే} (the \emph{ē}-sign) $\to$ \te{పే} (pē); \te{రు} (\emph{ru}). Read \te{పే}·\te{రు} $\to$ \emph{pēru}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pēru\textquotedblright{}
  \item its Dravidian cousins — \emph{pēru} / \emph{peyar} / \emph{pēr}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\te{పేరు}} native or a Sanskrit loan, and what Tamil word is its twin? (Native Dravidian, \emph{*pēr}; Tamil \emph{peyar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\te{న} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S109-letter-na}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ే} — what does it do?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{న}}
\textbf{\te{న}} — \emph{na}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{n}, it is \textbf{na}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{న} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{అవును}} \emph{avunu} — yes (avunu)
\end{itemize}

\section[nā]{\te{నా} (nā) — \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-naa}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}My\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian, no European cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)} \textbf{\te{న}} (na) + \textbf{\te{ా}} (long \emph{ā}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{నా}} (\emph{nā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{నా}} (\emph{nā}) means \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} It belongs to Telugu's native Dravidian first-person family, not to the Indo-European family behind English \emph{I/my}. You will meet the related word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} in its own lesson; today you only need \emph{nā}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{న} (\emph{na}) + \te{ా} (long ā) $\to$ \te{నా} (\emph{nā}).
\end{sounds}

\section[u]{\te{◌ు} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S02-vowel-sign-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{న} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{క}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ు}}
\textbf{\te{◌ు}} — \emph{u}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{u}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ు} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{అవును}} \emph{avunu} — yes (avunu)
  \item \textbf{\te{లేదు}} \emph{lēdu} — no / there isn't (lēdu)
  \item \textbf{\te{పేరు}} \emph{pēru} — name
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ు} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ు} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\section[nā pēru …]{\te{నా} \te{పేరు} … (nā pēru …) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…,\textquotedblright{} with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-naa-peru}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the two atoms — and note, as in Tamil and Kannada, no word for \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nā (my) + pēru (name) + your name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{పేరు} …} = \textquotedblleft{}my name …\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Nā pēru Arun.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the zero copula}]
There is \textbf{no verb}. Telugu sets \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} beside \textquotedblleft{}Arun\textquotedblright{} and lets the \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} be understood — the \textbf{zero copula} of the Dravidian family. \emph{Nā pēru Arun} = literally \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā pēru …\textquotedblright{} with your name
  \item notice — no word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Telugu. (\emph{Nā pēru ….}) What does Telugu leave out that English needs? (The verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — zero copula.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[1]{\te{౧} — the Telugu numeral for 1}

\label{lesson:TE-S140-digit-1}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ు} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{◌ా}?

One numeral this time, and it is read the way every numeral is read: as an amount.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{౧}}
Telugu writes its numbers twice. The digits you already use — 1, 2, 3 — are everywhere in modern Telugu, on price tags and phone screens. Beside them the language keeps \textbf{its own ten numerals}, and they have never gone away: they number the pages of Telugu books, they date the almanac, and they are painted on buses and doorplates.

\textbf{\te{౧}} is \textbf{one}.

You do not need a Telugu word for it yet. A numeral is read as a quantity, not as a sound, which is why this ladder can start here: the shape can be learned months before the word for it arrives.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{౧} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{౧} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

  \item \emph{Look:} for \te{౧} on any page of a Telugu book, calendar or doorplate you can find

\section[nuvvu / mīru]{\te{నువ్వు} / \te{మీరు} (nuvvu / mīru) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} familiar and respectful}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-nuvvu-miiru}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}You\textquotedblright{} — respect made the same way as Tamil, Kannada, and French.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)} \textbf{\te{నువ్వు}} (\emph{nuvvu}); \textbf{\te{మీరు}} (\emph{mīru}) = \textbf{\te{మీ}} (mī) + \textbf{\te{రు}} (ru).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{నువ్వు}} (\emph{nuvvu}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) traces to Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*nīn} — the same native root as Tamil \emph{nī} and Kannada \emph{nīnu}. \textbf{\te{మీరు}} (\emph{mīru}) is the respectful/plural \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: respect by the plural}]
\emph{nuvvu} (familiar) vs. \emph{mīru} (respectful, and literally plural) — the same politeness-by-plural as Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ}, Kannada \emph{nīvu}, and French \emph{vous}. For a first meeting, \textbf{mīru}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\te{నువ్వు} (\emph{nuvvu}); \te{మీరు} (\emph{mīru}, \te{మీ} \emph{mī} + \te{రు} \emph{ru}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nuvvu\textquotedblright{} (familiar), \textquotedblleft{}mīru\textquotedblright{} (respectful)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Telugu make \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} respectful, and which languages share the trick? (By the plural — \emph{mīru}; Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ}, Kannada \emph{nīvu}, French \emph{vous}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[virama]{\te{◌్} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S05-sign-virama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{౧} — what amount does it stand for? And one from further back: \te{◌ే}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌్}}
\textbf{\te{◌్}} — \emph{no sound of its own — it takes one away}.

It is a \textbf{vowel-killer}. Every consonant in this script arrives with an \emph{a} already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the \emph{a} back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌్} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{నువ్వు} / \te{మీరు}} \emph{nuvvu / mīru} — you (familiar / respectful)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌్} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌్} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌్} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}  ·  \te{అవును}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌్} three times, and each time say what it does: \textbf{it kills the built-in \emph{a}}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌్} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌్}? What does it do to the consonant it sits on? (\textbf{Takes away the built-in \emph{a}.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēmiṭi]{\te{ఏమిటి} (ēmiṭi) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-emiti}



\begin{quote}
The last piece of the question: \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)} \textbf{\te{ఏ}} (independent long \emph{ē}) + \textbf{\te{మి}} (mi) + \textbf{\te{టి}} (\emph{ṭi}, retroflex) $\to$ \textbf{ēmiṭi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{ఏమిటి}} (\emph{ēmiṭi}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative stem \textbf{*yā-/*e-} — the same Dravidian question-root as Tamil \emph{eṉṉa} and Kannada \emph{ēnu}, heading Telugu's question family: \emph{ēmiṭi} (what), \emph{evaru} (who), \emph{ekkaḍa} (where), \emph{enduku} (why).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{ఏ} (independent long ē) + \te{మి} (\emph{mi}) + \te{టి} (\emph{ṭi}, retroflex) $\to$ \emph{ēmiṭi}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ēmiṭi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the question family — ēmiṭi, evaru, ekkaḍa
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[2]{\te{౨} — the Telugu numeral for 2}

\label{lesson:TE-S141-digit-2}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌్} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{న}?

One numeral this time, and it is read the way every numeral is read: as an amount.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{౨}}
\textbf{\te{౨}} is \textbf{two}.

Two numerals now, and that is enough for the first real reading skill: telling them apart. A digit is never met alone on a page — it is met in a row of other digits, and the work is picking the one you want out of the row.

\section[mī pēru ēmiṭi?]{\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}? (mī pēru ēmiṭi?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-mii-peru-emiti}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the question — your + name + what — still no \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{మీ}} (\emph{mī}, \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) = the possessive of \emph{mīru} (\textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?} = literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what?}\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three words, \textbf{no verb} — the zero copula holds for questions too.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answer, and the familiar version}]
Answer with the sentence you built: \textbf{Nā pēru Arun.} The familiar \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} is \emph{nī} (from \emph{nuvvu}): \emph{nī pēru ēmiṭi?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mī pēru ēmiṭi?\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask, then answer — \textquotedblleft{}mī pēru ēmiṭi?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}nā pēru …\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?} literally say, and what's missing vs. English? (\textquotedblleft{}Your name what?\textquotedblright{}; no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — zero copula.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\te{◌ి} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S08-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{౨} — what amount does it stand for? And one from further back: \te{◌ు}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ి}}
\textbf{\te{◌ి}} — \emph{i}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{i}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ి} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?} \emph{mī pēru ēmiṭi?} — what is your name?
  \item \textbf{\te{ఏమిటి}} \emph{ēmiṭi} — what
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ి} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ి} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ి} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ఏమిటి}  ·  \te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}?  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ి} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ి} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ి}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{i} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣam]{\te{సంతోషం} (santōṣam) — \textquotedblleft{}joy,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-santosham}



\begin{quote}
The warm close — and, as in Kannada, a Sanskrit word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the full phrase}
The full form is \textbf{\te{మిమ్మల్ని} \te{కలిసినందుకు} \te{సంతోషం}} (\emph{mimmalni kalisinanduku santōṣam}) — \textquotedblleft{}joy at having met you.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{సంతోషం}} (\emph{santōṣam}, \textquotedblleft{}joy, gladness\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{Sanskrit} — \emph{sam-} (\textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{toṣa} (\textquotedblleft{}satisfaction\textquotedblright{}) — the \emph{same} loan Kannada uses (\emph{santōṣa}). Both reach for Sanskrit where Tamil keeps its native \emph{magiḻcci}. Telugu — the most Sanskritised of the four Dravidian tongues — does so most readily of all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}santōṣam\textquotedblright{}
  \item the split — Telugu/Kannada \emph{santōṣa(m)} (Sanskrit) vs. Tamil \emph{magiḻcci} (native)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\te{సంతోషం}} native or borrowed, and what does the contrast with Tamil show? (Sanskrit; Telugu borrows Sanskrit — here for \textquotedblleft{}pleased\textquotedblright{} — where Tamil keeps native \emph{magiḻcci}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anusvara]{\te{◌ం} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S04-sign-anusvara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ి} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{౧}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ం}}
\textbf{\te{◌ం}} — \emph{a nasal, ridden on the syllable before it}.

It is a \textbf{nasal}, written as a mark rather than as a letter. It rides on the syllable before it and turns the end of it nasal.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ం} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{సంతోషం}} — joy / pleased to meet you
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ం} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ం} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ం} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{సంతోషం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ం} three times, humming the nasal at the end of the syllable as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ం} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ం}? What does it add to the syllable before it? (\textbf{A nasal.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the introduction, whole}

\label{lesson:TE-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Everything you have met in this chapter, said once through as the exchange it was always for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the dialogue}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\te{నా} \te{పేరు} \te{మీరా}. (\emph{nā pēru Mira}) & My name is Mira. \\
\te{మీ} \te{పేరు} \te{ఏమిటి}? (\emph{mī pēru ēmiṭi}) & What's your name? \\
\te{నా} \te{పేరు} \te{అరుణ్}. (\emph{nā pēru Arun}) & My name is Arun. \\
\te{సంతోషం}. (\emph{santōṣam}) & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every atom traced:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pēru} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian \emph{*pēr} (\emph{not} \emph{name}; twin of Tamil \emph{peyar})
  \item \textbf{nā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nēnu} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{ēmiṭi} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian question-stem \emph{*yā-/*e-}
  \item \textbf{santōṣam} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Sanskrit} (Telugu borrows for \textquotedblleft{}pleased\textquotedblright{}; Tamil keeps native \emph{magiḻcci})
\end{itemize}

The Telugu habit: the \textbf{zero copula} (no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item your own introduction — \textquotedblleft{}nā pēru …\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it back — \textquotedblleft{}mī pēru ēmiṭi?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name, ask someone else's, say you're pleased. (\emph{Nā pēru …. / Mī pēru ēmiṭi? / Santōṣam.}) Which word is Sanskrit, not native? (\emph{santōṣam}.)

Next chapter: \emph{elā unnāru?} (\textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}) and answering with \emph{bāgunnānu} — the responding cycle.
\end{tcolorbox}
